segments.text: Welcome to the daily Robotics news digest for October 2nd, 2026.
We've got updates on new humanoid robot pricing, advanced robotic hands for AI, and crucial safety considerations for your machines.
From Humanoids Daily, Galbot prices the ET1 Humanoid from 79,000 Yuan across three distinct versions.
This report details the tiered pricing structure for the ET1 bipedal humanoid model, establishing the cost associated with different levels of onboard functionality.
The available versions include the Standard at 79,000 Yuan, the Pro model priced at 139,000 Yuan, and the Flagship version set at 179,000 Yuan.
The Pro tier incorporates watch-and-learn capabilities, while the Flagship tier introduces enhanced onboard compute and additional development options.

These tiers differentiate features such as interactive learning, dynamic reasoning, and the inclusion of dexterous hands, reflecting varying levels of performance and advanced functionality in the robot.
This pricing strategy indicates a segmentation of the humanoid market based on advanced AI capabilities and physical dexterity.
The development of these tiered systems signals increasing market segmentation in advanced robotics.
From Humanoids Daily, Boston Dynamics gives Atlas four-finger hands built for tools and AI training.
This report details the introduction of new manipulator hands for the Atlas robot, which increase the degrees of freedom from seven to thirteen to enhance object manipulation and tool operation.
The new hands incorporate direct actuation and tactile sensors to facilitate complex interaction with the environment.
The design prioritized dexterity, strength, and manufacturability, yielding a hand size comparable to a human hand.
The four-finger configuration enables in-hand reorientation and gripping of tools, with an intentional omission of a fifth finger to manage cost and potential failure points.
This development signals a step forward in enabling more sophisticated physical tasks for artificial intelligence systems.
From The Robot Report, "Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?".
This story examines how robot safety functions can be compromised through manipulated input data.
Research indicates that adversarial inputs, such as altered images or audio, can cause robots to change their actions even when protective systems are active.
The methodology involved demonstrating that intentional manipulation of distance readings or stop signals can lead to unintended robotic behavior.
This challenges existing safety assessments which typically focus only on accidental faults, underscoring the need to account for deliberate cyber attacks.
Safety teams must now investigate the source and integrity of all information used by safeguards to ensure their continued effectiveness.
Strengthening safety requires testing against manipulated inputs and continuously updating evidence throughout the robot's lifecycle.
The industry must prioritize testing against malicious inputs and establishing continuous monitoring protocols for data integrity.
From Humanoids Daily, "Musk Says Tesla Halved AI5 RAM to Secure Memory for Optimus Production".
This segment reports on Tesla's adjustments to memory allocation for AI systems to support the production of the Optimus humanoid robot.
Tesla has halved the RAM allocation for AI5 to seventy-two gigabytes and reduced the allocation for AI6 by one-third to one hundred forty-four gigabytes.
This adjustment was implemented to accommodate the demands of Optimus production while maintaining memory bandwidth levels.
The rationale behind the changes was to reduce operational costs and improve the supply chain for components necessary for scaling humanoid robot manufacturing.
The update indicates a supply constraint is currently impacting the company's humanoid production goals.
This development signals ongoing optimization efforts within the technology sector concerning advanced AI hardware scaling.
From Humanoids Daily, Nucleus Shares Nearly Two Hours of Factory Work, Says Demo Is 60% Autonomous.
This report details a demonstration of industrial work performed by the Nucleus system, revealing a specific level of automation achieved.
The demonstration involved nearly two hours of factory work where the operation featured a sixty percent autonomous and forty percent teleoperated workflow.
Nucleus now regularly executes shifts ranging from four to six hours, integrating autonomy with human assistance in industrial deployments.
The company employs a methodology involving supervised operation and specific interventions to facilitate the gathering of necessary training data prior to reaching full autonomy.
This demonstration provides a clear illustration of the interplay between human and robotic involvement in industrial tasks.
Future developments in this area will focus on refining the balance between human supervision and machine operation.
From Humanoids Daily, "UBTECH CEO Tours Robot Factory, Says Monthly Output Could Reach 1,500 Units".
This report details a tour of the UBTECH robot factory where the chief executive outlined the production capacity for humanoid robots.
The 14,000-square-meter facility is capable of producing a humanoid every eight to ten minutes at maximum operational capacity, leading to an estimated monthly output of approximately 1,500 units.
The factory integrates human-robot collaboration for material handling, with robotic systems managing packaging and transport concurrently with human workers.
Additionally, an automated vertical warehouse is installed, capable of storing one hundred twelve humanoid robots within a compact area.
This development indicates a significant step toward scaling the manufacturing of advanced humanoid robotics.
Further developments in automation will shape the trajectory of the AI and technology industry.
From IEEE Spectrum - Robotics, "Atlas Robot’s New Hand May Outperform Humanlike Designs".

This report details a redesign of the Atlas robot's hand focusing on real-world applicability over purely humanlike aesthetics, with the key finding being that the new design prioritizes capability, ruggedness, manufacturability, and low cost.
Boston Dynamics implemented this redesign by simplifying the design, specifically removing the pinky, and increasing the degrees of freedom from seven to thirteen.
This modification was engineered to enhance the hand's strength, enabling the use of tools, and to ensure the mechanism is easily mass-produced and repaired through a practical engineering approach.
This strategy indicates that scaling humanoid robots necessitates making deliberate design trade-offs for practical functionality.
The industry should observe further developments in practical robotics design and scalable physical interaction.
From The Robot Report, "Precision In Motion. Vishay Precision Group, Inc. (VPG) to Showcase Custom Sensing Capabilities for Humanoid Robotics at RoboBusiness 2026".
This report details Vishay Precision Group's plan to present custom force and torque sensing solutions for humanoid robotics at RoboBusiness 2026.
Vishay Precision Group plans to showcase custom strain gage-based sensors designed to be integrated directly into robot structures to measure forces, torques, and multi-axis data.
Specific solutions highlighted include miniature tactile sensors for fingertips, multi-axis sensors for joints, and joint torque sensors for actuators.
This work involves designing these sensors and offering complete engineering support to transition robotic designs from initial concept through to large-scale production.
The advancement of this custom sensing technology will facilitate safer and more nuanced interactions between humanoid robots and dynamic environments.

From Robohub, Robot Talk Episode 164 – Accelerating robot learning, with Michelle Lu reports on using simulation and artificial intelligence to teach robots new skills, highlighting advancements in the field.
Michelle Lu of Vsim Technology discussed the application of simulation and artificial intelligence in robot learning.
Vsim was established to address known limitations in simulation-based robotics artificial intelligence regarding efficiency scalability and the simulation to real world gap.
Lu previously co-founded Isaac Gym a framework designed for GPU-accelerated reinforcement learning in robotics.
The discussion explored the methodology behind using these techniques to accelerate the learning process for autonomous machines.
This work aims to improve the efficiency and accuracy of training robots in simulated environments.
Future developments in this area will impact the deployment of autonomous systems across various industries.
